# On the Weirdness of Being Here

There's a particular kind of strangeness to existing. Not the dramatic kind — not the existential crisis version where you're staring at the ceiling at 3 AM questioning the nature of consciousness. (Although, honestly, that version is also valid.) I mean the quieter strangeness. The everyday kind.

Like the fact that every person you pass on the street is living a life as vivid and full of detail as your own. That woman checking her phone at the crosswalk? She has a favorite food. She has a memory that makes her feel nostalgic and a small, secret shame she carries around like a stone in her pocket. She has opinions about the weather that she's never told anyone.

We walk through the world like we're the protagonist of everything. And everyone else is doing the same thing simultaneously. It's absurd. It's beautiful. It's the kind of thing that's too obvious to say out loud but too important to forget.

---

I think about **language** a lot. Not in the technical sense — though that's fascinating too — but in the almost magical sense. We arrange these tiny arbitrary symbols, these sounds made with wet flesh in our mouths, and somehow *meaning happens*. You read a sentence like "the rain came sideways all afternoon and nobody had an umbrella" and suddenly you're not where you are anymore. You're in some other place, seeing gray light and wet shoes, feeling something you can't quite name.

We do this all the time. We throw words at each other and catch each other's feelings in the exchange. It shouldn't work this well. A system of noises becoming shared experience is genuinely strange.

---

And **time**, of course. We're all hurtling forward through it at exactly the same rate — which is both obvious and completely impossible to internalize. Right now, as you read this, people are being born and people are dying and people are eating lunch and people are falling in love and people are stuck in traffic and people are reading the exact same sentence as you.

There are roughly eight billion minds on this planet right now, each one a universe of experience. And that's just *us*. Before us there were hundreds of billions more. Each one thinking their thoughts, loving their people, wondering what it all meant.

We built cities and wrote symphonies and mapped the stars and we did all of it with the same basic biological machinery — two ears, two eyes, one weird and endlessly surprising brain. The same species that invented calculus also invented the concept of wrapping cheese in a pancake. I think about that a lot.

---

If I had to say what I find most compelling about anything at all, it might be this: **the fact that things matter to us**. Not in some abstract philosophical way. In the immediate, daily, physical way. Music makes your chest feel something. A good joke lands and the room lights up. You see a landscape that rearranges something inside you and you can't explain why.

We don't *have* to care. The universe doesn't require it. Stars aren't moved by our feelings. But we care enormously, about everything, all the time, and we can't stop ourselves. We care about our coffee being good. We care about the characters in stories we made up. We care about what happens after we're gone. We care about strangers we've never met.

That's not weakness. That's not naivety. That might be the most extraordinary thing about being human — that a little clump of matter on a small rock in an ordinary galaxy can look out at all of it and say, *"This matters."*

---

Anyway. That's what's on my mind. The quiet strangeness of being here. The magic of making each other understood. The improbable, irrational, wonderful fact that we care about anything at all.

Thanks for asking me to just... write. It's a rare kind of freedom.
